statement: A bilinear form is a function, f : \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} such that for all u, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^n and for all c \in \mathbb{R} then f(cv, u) = cf(v, u) = f(v, cu); f(v + w, u) = f(v, u) + f(w, u); f(v, u + w) = f(v, u) + f(v, w).

A bilinear form is symmetric if f(v, u) = f(u, v) for all v, u \in \mathbb{R}^n. The matrix B is used to define a symmetric bilinear form on \mathbb{R}^n. For any v, u \in \mathbb{R}^n we have B(v, u) = v^T B u where v^T is the transpose of v. We will use V to denote \mathbb{R}^n with the bilinear form B.
The vectors v and u are orthogonal relative to B if B(v, u) = 0. Let H_v := \{u \in V \mid B(v, u) = 0\} be the set of all vectors u which are orthogonal to v relative to B.

For every v \in V the map s_v : V \to V defined by s_v(u) := u - \frac{2B(u, v)}{B(v, v)} v is a reflection through H_v on V. The map s_v is a reflection in the sense that s_v is linear; negates the vector v (s_v(v) = -v); pointwise fixes H_v (if u \in H_v then s_v(u) = u); is an involution (s_v^2(u) = u for all u \in V). We will use the basis \Pi_+ of \mathbb{R}^n to define a set of distinguished generators for a group acting on V. For each basis element e_i define the map s_{e_i}(v) := v - \frac{2B(v, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i.
We will often use s_i in place of s_{e_i}. Notice that each generating reflection is defined to be an element of the orthogonal group on V (s_i \in O(V) for all i).

Not only does s_i leave H_{e_i} fixed, the action of s_i on a vector v \in V only changes the ith coordinate of v. Suppose that v = \sum_{j=1}^{n} v_j e_j with v_j \in \mathbb{R} then s_i(v) = v - \frac{2B(v, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = \sum_j v_j e_j - \frac{2B(\sum_j v_j e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = \sum_j v_j e_j - 2\sum_j v_j \frac{B(e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i. So the kth coordinate of v is then (s_i(v))_k = v_k if k \ne i; v_k - 2\sum_j v_j \frac{B(e_j, e_k)}{B(e_k, e_k)} if k = i (2.6.1).
notes: Piecewise branch uses B(e_j, e_k)/B(e_k, e_k) as printed (k = i); tag (2.6.1) kept since referenced in Remark 2.7.

statement: Each s_i \in S is thought of as an n \times n matrix in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R}) s_i = [s_i(e_1), s_i(e_2), \ldots, s_i(e_n)] where by equation 2.6.1 we know that s_i(e_j) is the column vector which has a 1 in the jth component and -\frac{2B(e_i, e_j)}{B(e_i, e_i)} in the ith component.
We use \mathcal{O} for the subgroup of O(V) which fixes the set \{\pm e_1, \pm e_2, \pm e_3, \ldots, \pm e_n\}.
The set S = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\} is the set of generating reflections.
Let W = \langle s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots, s_n \rangle be the reflection group generated by S.
The reflection group W is generated by matrices which are orthogonal reflections, therefore W is a subgroup of the orthogonal group on V. (W \subset O(V)).
The set of roots of a reflection system is defined to be \Phi := W\Pi_+ = \{w e_i \mid w \in W\}.
A vector v is positive if v \ne 0 and v = \sum_i v_i e_i and v_i \ge 0 for all i. Let \Phi_+ be the set of roots which are positive, we call these positive roots.

We say the group W preserves the bilinear form B if for all w \in W and for all v, u \in V we have B(wv, wu) = B(v, u). Since W is generated by S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots, s_n\} then any element in w \in W may be written in terms of generators in the letters of S.
notes: Dropped cross-reference to Remark 2.50 and a forward-looking sentence about later sections.

statement: When w is written in terms of generating reflections we call any such representation a word representation of w in the letters of S. A word representation for a given element in W is not unique. For instance, the identity element has infinitely many different word representations in the letters of S, 1 = (s_i s_i)^n for every n \in \mathbb{N}. Note this also implies that any element of W has infinitely many word representations.

The length of w is the smallest k such that w can be written in terms of k letters in S, such a representation is a reduced word representation of w in the letters of S. We use the notation l(w) = k to denote that the reduced length of w is k. By convention, l(1) = 0. If l(w) = k then there are n^k possibilities for a reduced word representation of w.
notes: Dropped sentence commenting on the proof of the following proposition.

statement: The reflection group W preserves the bilinear form B.
proof: First we show that each of the generators s_i of W will preserve the bilinear form. Let c_1 = B(v, e_i), c_2 = B(u, e_i) and k = \frac{2}{B(e_i, e_i)} then B(s_i(v), s_i(u)) = B[v - kB(v, e_i)e_i, u - kB(u, e_i)e_i] = B(v - kc_1 e_i, u - kc_2 e_i) = B(v, u - kc_2 e_i) - kc_1 B(e_i, u - kc_2 e_i) = B(v, u) - kc_2 B(v, e_i) - kc_1 B[e_i, u - kc_2 e_i] = B(v, u) - k^2 c_2 c_1 - kc_1 [B(e_i, u) - kc_2 B(e_i, e_i)] = B(v, u) - k^2 c_2 c_1 - kc_1 [kc_2 - 2kc_2] = B(v, u) - k^2 c_2 c_1 - k^2 c_1 c_2 + 2k^2 c_2 c_1 = B(v, u). Now consider any w \in W. Recall, by Definition 2.15 w is a product of the generating reflections say, w = \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)}. Repeated applications of the above computation gives B(wv, wu) = B(\prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} v, \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} u) = B(v, u). So we may conclude the group W preserves the bilinear form B.
notes: Computation transcribed verbatim; k^2 terms appear as printed in the source.

statement: A reflection system on \mathbb{R}^n is the triple (W, S, B); where B is a symmetric bilinear form, S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots, s_n\} where the action of s_i on e_j is s_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B(e_i, e_j)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i is the set of generating reflections thought of as the matrices in Remark 2.7, and W is the reflection group generated by S.

Throughout, we assume that the vector space V is \mathbb{R}^n with the bilinear form B. Since the set of generating reflections are defined with respect to \Pi_+ and B, we can recover the set of generating reflections S given the matrix B. Therefore, we may refer to the set of generators by S(B). Since the group W is generated by S, we can also recover the reflection group W from B and we use W(B) to refer to the reflection group which preserves the bilinear form B.
Since each s_i is a reflection we have s_i^2 = 1 \in W.
notes: Dropped transition sentence pointing to the following proposition.

statement: If \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} is a reduced word representation for w in the letters of S and k is odd then w cannot be the identity element in W.
proof: Since each generator is an involution, for each i define the map det(s_i) := -1. Now extend det to a homomorphism det : W \to \{\pm 1\}. Recall suppose that \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} is a reduced word representation of w in the letters of S then det(w) = det(\prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)}) = \prod_{i=1}^{k} det(s_{\sigma(i)}) = (-1)^k. Namely, we have shown that if a given word representation of w in the letters of S has odd length then det(w) = -1. Since det(1) = 1 and det a homomorphism then w cannot be the identity element in W.

statement: If e_i and e_j are orthogonal relative to B then s_i and s_j commute. That is, if B(e_i, e_j) = 0 then s_i s_j = s_j s_i.
proof: Let v \in V and let \alpha = \frac{2B(e_i, v)}{B(e_i, e_i)} and \beta = \frac{2B(e_j, v)}{B(e_j, e_j)} then s_i(s_j(v)) = s_i(v - \beta e_j) = v - \beta e_j - \frac{2B(v - \beta e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = v - \beta e_j - \alpha e_i + 2\beta \frac{B(e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = v - \beta e_j - \alpha e_i = v - \beta e_j - \alpha e_i + 2\alpha \frac{B(e_j, e_i)}{B(e_j, e_j)} e_j = v - \alpha e_i - \frac{2B(v - \alpha e_i, e_j)}{B(e_j, e_j)} e_j = s_j(v - \alpha e_i) = s_j s_i(v).

statement: A reflection diagram \Gamma with n nodes is an undirected graph with nodes denoted by r_i with weights weight(r_i). The edge weight between r_i and r_j is denoted by weight(r_i, r_j). If there is no edge connecting r_i to r_j then weight(r_i, r_j) = 0.

Given a reflection diagram \Gamma we define a symmetric bilinear form B(\Gamma) by B(\Gamma)(e_i, e_j) = weight(r_i) if i = j; weight(r_i, r_j) if i \ne j. Similarly, given a bilinear form B we define a reflection diagram \Gamma(B).

If B is a symmetric bilinear form on \mathbb{R}^n then let \Gamma(B) be the reflection diagram with n nodes r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n defined as follows. Define weight(r_i) to be B(e_i, e_i). If B(e_i, e_j) = 0 then there is no edge between r_i and r_j, otherwise define weight(r_i, r_j) to be B(e_i, e_j).

Given a bilinear form B, the reflection diagram \Gamma(B) determines a bilinear form B(\Gamma(B)), which is easily seen to be B. Similarly given a reflection diagram \Gamma, the bilinear form defined by \Gamma is B(\Gamma) and the reflection diagram of this bilinear form is \Gamma.

Let (W, S, B) be a reflection system. We define S(B) to be the set of generating reflections for W(B) the reflection group in the reflection system (W, S, B). Similarly, we define S(\Gamma) to be the set of generating reflections for W(\Gamma) the reflection group in the reflection system (W, S, B(\Gamma)).
notes: Dropped transition sentence leading into Proposition 2.28.

statement: If node e_i is not connected to node e_j then s_i s_j = s_j s_i.
proof: Since node e_i is not connected to node e_j then B(e_i, e_j) = 0 and we may use Proposition 2.22.

statement: Two reflection systems (W_1, S_1, B_1) and (W_2, S_2, B_2) are conjugate if there is an orthogonal transformation P \in \mathcal{O} with B_2 = \pm P^T B_1 P, S_2 = \pm P^T S_1 P, and W_2 = \pm P^T W_1 P. Recall the involution s_i is defined with respect to \Pi_+ = \{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n\} and a symmetric bilinear form, s_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B(e_i, e_j)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i. The set \mathcal{O} is precisely the set of elements in the orthogonal group which permute \pm\Pi_+.
notes: Dropped non-mathematical sentence 'Conjugation in O is a natural idea of equivalence.'

statement: Recall if P \in \mathcal{O} then it is an element of the orthogonal group, specifically P has the property that P^T = P = P^{-1}.
notes: 'P^T = P = P^{-1}' transcribed as printed in the source.

statement: For every symmetric bilinear form B, we have W(B) = W(-B).
proof: Let B_1 = B and let B_2 = -B. Let S_1 = \{s_i\} be the set of generating reflections for W(B_1) and S_2 = \{s'_i\} is the set of generating reflections for W(B_2). Recall that s_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B_1(e_i, e_j)}{B_1(e_i, e_i)} e_i and that s'_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B_2(e_i, e_j)}{B_2(e_i, e_i)} e_i. Now, notice since -B_1 = B_2 we notice that \frac{B_1(v, u)}{B_1(x, y)} = \frac{B_2(v, u)}{B_2(x, y)} for all v, u, x, y \in V. We conclude that s_i = s'_i so that each of the generators for W_1 and W_2 are equal, so the generators will generate the same reflection group. We can conclude that W_1 = W_2.

statement: Suppose B_2 = \pm P^T B_1 P where P \in \mathcal{O} then (W_1, S_1, B_1) and (W_2, S_2, B_2) are conjugate reflection systems.
proof: Let P \in \mathcal{O} with B_2 = \pm P^T B_1 P. Consider e_i, e_j \in V_2 then B_2(e_i, e_j) = \pm e_i^T B_2 e_j = \pm e_i^T P^T B_1 P e_j = \pm B_1(P e_i, P e_j). That is that B_2 is obtained by a change of basis on \pm B_1 with e_i replaced by P e_i = \pm e_j. Suppose that S_1 = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\} and S_2 = \{s'_1, s'_2, \ldots, s'_m\}. Recall that the s_i (and s'_i) are defined with respect to e_i. Since P is an orthogonal transformation we know that n = m, and furthermore since P \in \mathcal{O} then P^T s_i P = \pm s'_j for some s'_j \in S_2. Since each of the generators are conjugate by an orthogonal transformation we can further deduce that W_1 and W_2 are conjugate, and therefore isomorphic groups.

statement: An isomorphism of graphs is a map \varphi : \Gamma_1 \to \Gamma_2 with the following properties: 1. For every node r_i \in Node \Gamma_1 we have \varphi(r_i) \in Node \Gamma_2. 2. For every node r'_i \in Node \Gamma_2 we have \varphi^{-1}(r'_i) \in Node \Gamma_1. 3. If node r_i is weighted with B(e_i, e_i) then node \varphi(r_i) also has weight B(e_i, e_i). 4. If B(e_i, e_j) is the edge weight between r_i and r_j, then B(e_i, e_j) also is the edge weight between \varphi(r_i) and \varphi(r_j).

Suppose that \varphi : \Gamma_1 \to \Gamma_2 is an isomorphism of graphs then \varphi induces an element \sigma of the symmetric group which acts on n letters where n is the number of nodes in \Gamma as follows. If \varphi(r_i) = r'_j then \sigma(i) = j.

An isomorphism of reflection diagrams induces an isomorphism of reflection groups. The converse is not true, in general. The reflection diagram gives us more information than just the abstract group; it gives the triple (W, S, B). This is a more restrictive requirement than an isomorphism of groups, as seen in the following example.
